title: Civilian agency 'one model' to probe police-custody deaths
article: The head of the Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP is playing down the need for an independent civilian agency in British Columbia to investigate deaths that occur in police custody.
A system in place in Ontario since 1990 was described as "one model," by Paul Kennedy during a visit to Vancouver yesterday.

The Ontario Special Investigations Unit is a civilian law-enforcement agency that is called in whenever there is a serious injury or death involving police and civilians in the province. The unit has the power to file criminal charges, which are prosecuted by a special branch of the Ministry of the Attorney-General.

"There are nine other jurisdictions that don't have that model. That is one of many models. People have to decide what is appropriate," Mr. Kennedy said after meeting with the B.C. Civil Liberties Association.

"Clearly, there has been an increased appetite for more civilian oversight," said Mr. Kennedy, who was appointed chair of the complaints commission in October and who previously served as a senior lawyer in the federal Justice Department and as counsel to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. The issue of whether "police can investigate themselves is still an ongoing debate," he suggested.

The civil-liberties group held a news conference yesterday to ask the complaints commission to order hearings into the deaths of four men who were being pursued by RCMP or were in RCMP custody in British Columbia in the past 14 months.
Kevin St. Arnaud, fatally shot by an RCMP officer investigating a robbery in Vanderhoof in December.
Gurmeet Sandhu, who died in Surrey last June after police used a taser on him.

Ian Bush, 22, shot and killed by an RCMP officer in October after a scuffle broke out at the police station. He had been taken into custody after giving the wrong name to an officer who was pouring out his beer at a local hockey game.
Ryan Snopek, 30, who died in custody in Cranbrook on New Year's Day after being arrested for public intoxication the previous evening.

All of the deaths are being investigated by RCMP officers from outside the local detachments. The force also conducts an internal review and once the investigations are complete, the provincial coroner is required to call an inquest.
Coroner's inquests rarely begin until many months after a death and are not allowed to assess blame when it comes to a police officer's actions.
"In-house investigations, the results of which will not be shared with the public, create fertile soil for a cover-up," said Jason Gratl, president of the civil-liberties association.
"There has to be some level of independent oversight," said the association's executive director, Murray Mollard.
Creston Mayor Joe Snopek, the uncle of Ryan Snopek, echoed the concerns and said there should be independent probes of deaths in police custody.
"I am a big supporter of the RCMP. They have a tough job to do." But he said he would like an "outside look" at his nephew's death rather than "having the RCMP look at the RCMP."
